intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.

checks.claim: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia of the Sedaghatian type (SMDS) is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Our identification of truncating mutations in GPX4 in two families affected with SSMD supports the pathogenic role of mutated GPX4 in this very rare disease.
checks.explanation: The abstract shows that one child had two different GPX4 variants (one maternal, one de novo). In the second family, only the parents were tested, and both carried the same variant. No child is shown to be homozygous, so the 'homozygous' part is inferred rather than shown.

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia is a neonatal lethal form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. It is characterized by severe metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with mild limb shortening, platyspondyly, cardiac conduction defects, and central nervous system abnormalities (summary by Smith et al., 2014).

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian (1980) reported 2 brothers, born within a year of each other, who had a similar skeletal disorder with severe congenital metaphyseal involvement, mild rhizomelic shortness of the upper limbs, and mild platyspondyly. Both died at 3 days of age of cardiorespiratory insufficiency. Only 1 of the brothers had laboratory tests before death, which showed low calcium, high phosphorus, and high alkaline phosphatase levels, attributed to a renal defect. At autopsy, this infant had pulmonary, renal, and adrenal hemorrhage, as well as subendocardial myocarditis and myocardial necrosis. The parents were normal and had recently had an affected baby girl.

They also noted that the Iranian infant reported by Opitz et al. (1987) had a similar perinatal course and similar radiographs.

paragraphs.text: Koutouby et al. (2000) reported an infant born to nonconsanguineous Yemeni parents who had radiologic findings consistent with Sedaghatian-type lethal metaphyseal chondrodysplasia. All earlier reported patients had died within 4 days of life, but this patient survived 161 days. The patient underwent extensive investigation, including serum calcium, magnesium, zinc, ammonia, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathormone levels, liver and renal function tests, TORCH studies, metabolic screening, skeletal survey, chromosome studies, muscle enzymes, EEG, and CT and MRI of the brain.

paragraphs.text: English et al. (2006) reported a girl, born to nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents, with metaphyseal dysplasia and a neuronal migration abnormality, consistent with Sedaghatian spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. She was hypotonic from birth and had recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. Brain imaging showed absence of the corpus callosum and marked frontotemporal pachygyria. She developed seizures on day 14 of life and died at 17 days of age. English et al. (2006) suggested that neuronal migration abnormalities may occur in this disorder and that agenesis of the corpus callosum is a novel association.

paragraphs.text: As part of the FORGE Canada Consortium, Smith et al. (2014) studied 2 unrelated families with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. Whole-exome sequencing of an affected girl and her unaffected parents identified 2 rare variants in the GPX4 gene: a c.587+5G-A change inherited from the mother and a de novo deletion (c.588-8_588-4del). Both variants were predicted to affect splicing. In vitro studies confirmed that the c.587+5G-A mutation caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out and that the deletion caused skipping of exon 5. In both cases this led to a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4. In a second family, DNA from the affected child was not available, but Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents were heterozygous for the same nonsense mutation in exon 3 of GPX4 (c.381C-A, tyr127-to-ter, Y127X).
